title: "Term Project — The Pump Station"
---

One design problem, run like the real thing: a client, a budget, a catalog,
three traps, and a two-page memo that has to survive a hostile reading.
Everything you've built this semester — the head equation, NPSH, affinity,
specific speed, and the toolbox — gets used in anger.

## The client's letter

> The town of Ralston Draw, Colorado (elev. ~1700 m — design at **83 kPa**
> atmospheric) is replacing its river-intake pump station. Water must be
> lifted from the intake gallery to the storage tank on the mesa:
> **48 m of static lift** through **1.8 km** of new commercial-steel main
> (route fixed; you choose the diameter from standard sizes: 150, 200, or
> 250 mm). The intake gallery puts the pump deck **2.0 m above** river
> low-water. Suction-side: 6 m of pipe, sharp entrance, strainer.
> Discharge side: six 90° elbows, a swing check valve, free exit into the
> tank.
>
> **Demand:** 25 L/s average (6,000 h/yr) and **40 L/s peak** (2,000 h/yr).
> The station must meet peak. District policy: **NPSH margin ≥ 1.0 m at
> every operating condition** (our last station taught us why), electricity
> at \$0.13/kWh, evaluation horizon **10 years**.
>
> Propose the pipe diameter and the machine plan — model(s), how many, how
> arranged, how controlled at average demand. We will read the memo, not
> your code.

## Your catalog

The district buys from one supplier. In the toolbox:

```python
from fluidtools.pipeflow import pump_catalog, catalog_report
catalog_report()          # the one-pager
pumps = pump_catalog()    # ready-to-use Pump objects (.price, .rpm attached)
```

Eight machines, from a \$1,400 utility pump to a \$21,000 axial monster.
Before you compute anything, run each one's specific speed past the habitat
map from module 10.2 — most of the catalog eliminates itself, and your memo
should say so in one sentence rather than eight.

## Milestones (graded checkpoints)

**M1 — after Unit 8 (weeks 10–11): the system, characterized.** Flow curves
for all three candidate diameters ($H$ required vs. $Q$, static + friction),
each with one paragraph: what the 48 m of gravity costs, what each diameter's
friction adds at peak, and which loss category dominates. No pumps yet.

**M2 — after module 10.2 (week 13): the machine plan.** Candidate
architectures evaluated *at the operating point the curves actually give
you* — single machine, series, parallel, speed-controlled — each with flow
delivered, NPSH margin (at 83 kPa!), and shaft power. Kill the failures
explicitly; a rejected option with a stated reason is worth as much as the
winner.

**M3 — finals week: the memo.** Two pages to the district: recommendation,
10-year cost (capital + energy, both duty points weighted by hours), the
margin table, and one honest paragraph titled **"What would make me wrong"**
— the assumption your design leans on hardest, and what happens if it
slips. Code as an appendix notebook the district's engineer could re-run.

## The rules of engagement

- The 1.0 m NPSH policy is not negotiable, and it applies at **every**
  condition you propose to run — including the clever low-flow ones.
- "Meets peak" means meets it with the policy margin, not grazes it.
- Money talks in 10-year totals. A pump that saves \$8,000 in energy is
  allowed to cost more than a pump that doesn't.
- Oversizing is a finding, not a safety factor. If your station can deliver
  60 L/s the town never asked for, the memo should either defend that
  headroom or spend it.

::: {.callout-important}
## Fair warning (this is the entire hint you get)
At least one obvious-looking design meets the flow requirement and fails the
mission anyway; at least one "upgrade" makes things worse; and one textbook
architecture from Unit 10 dies here for a reason the same unit taught you.
The traps are not hidden — they fall out of the same three lines of toolbox
code as everything else. Run the checks *before* you fall in love with a
design.
:::

## Deliverables & grading

| Item | Weight | What earns it |
|---|---|---|
| M1 system characterization | 15% | correct curves; loss anatomy in words |
| M2 architecture screen | 25% | every candidate has an operating point, a margin, and a verdict |
| M3 memo | 40% | a decision a professional could sign: numbers, tradeoffs, the "wrong" paragraph |
| Appendix notebook | 10% | runs top-to-bottom on a clean install |
| Peer red-team review | 10% | you get a classmate's M2; find one thing they missed (kindly) |

Work in pairs. Both names on the memo means both of you can defend any
number in it — I will pick one of you and one number at random during the
M3 sign-off, and it will be a friendly conversation only if the number
holds up.
